power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Purpose.
Postpartum depression (PPD) disproportionately affects women experiencing socioeconomic hardship.
We examined the association between exposure to Rx Kids, the nation's first universal and unconditional perinatal cash transfer program, and PPD risk among mothers of one-month-old infants.
Methods.

This study used Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) data collected from electronic health records of 815 one-month well-child visits between 2022 and 2025, spanning two years before and after Rx Kids implementation.

Difference-in-differences analyses compared changes in depression screening outcomes among mothers residing in Flint, Michigan, where Rx Kids was implemented, with changes among mothers residing outside Flint.
In the two years before Rx Kids, the prevalence of high risk PPD scores > 13 was 8.7% in Flint and 6.2% outside Flint; two years after, the prevalence was 3.3% in Flint and 10.4% outside Flint.

text.text: Rx Kids exposure was associated with a 9.8-percentage-point reduction in high risk PPD scores (95% CI, -16.8 to -2.8, p = 0.006), reversing the preexisting geographic disparity.
Reductions were also observed in moderate PPD risk and mean EPDS scores.

Findings suggest that universal and unconditional perinatal cash support may be an effective upstream strategy for preventing PPD, improving maternal mental health, and reducing place-based disparities.

Postpartum depression (PPD) is a common and increasingly prevalent maternal mental health condition with significant consequences for mothers, infants, and families. [1] [2] [3] [4] PPD is associated with adverse maternal health outcomes, impaired mother-infant bonding, and poorer child developmental outcomes. [5] [6] [7] Its burden is not equally distributed, with disparities associated with race and ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and preexisting health conditions. 3, 4 Efforts to address PPD have largely focused on detection and treatment.

text.text: Beyond its consequences for maternal and infant health, 5 PPD also imposes substantial economic costs through increased healthcare expenditures, lost productivity, and adverse developmental outcomes for children, among other costs. 11 Policies that strengthen family economic security during the perinatal period may therefore improve maternal mental health while reducing downstream health and economic costs.

text.text: Launched in January 2024 in Flint, Michigan, Rx Kids is the nation's first universal, place-based, unconditional cash prescription program that begins prenatally and extends through infancy. 12 Designed to improve population-level maternal and infant health by reducing the harmful effects of poverty during a critical developmental period, Rx Kids prescribes a one-time $1,500 payment mid-pregnancy, then $500 monthly during infancy.

text.text: Rx Kids has been associated with measurable improvements in family financial stability, maternal and infant health, and family well-being. [13] [14] [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] Previous survey-based Rx Kids research found a 14.0-percentage-point reduction in positive depression screens using the CES-D-10 among postpartum mothers. 13 This study builds on earlier findings by examining whether exposure to Rx Kids was associated with reduced PPD risk using data from electronic health records, as measured by the EPDS during one-month well-child pediatric visits.

text.text: Using a quasi-experimental difference-indifferences study design, we evaluated changes in PPD risk before and after Rx Kids implementation within and outside Flint, Michigan.

By examining the effects of population-wide unconditional perinatal cash support on PPD risk, this study allows us to examine whether upstream economic policies may be an important tool for improving maternal mental health, complementing clinical care strategies, and advancing maternal and infant health equity.

Flint, Michigan, is a majority-minority city and represents a high-risk, structurally disadvantaged setting where poverty, housing instability, and economic stress are strongly linked to adverse maternal and infant health outcomes, with clear geographic disparities in these outcomes when compared with nearby communities and statewide metrics. [20] [21] [22] Hurley Children's Clinic in Flint is a high-volume pediatric primary care clinic and the medical home to 1,226 infants from 2022-2025, 87.4% of whom were born at the affiliated hospital, Hurley Medical Center, and approximately 88% of whom were insured by Medicaid.

text.text: For this quasi-experimental difference-in-differences study, data were abstracted from electronic health records.

The study included 815 mothers who gave birth at Hurley Medical Center between 01/01/2022 and 12/31/2025 and who completed the EPDS at their infant's onemonth well-child visit (i.e., occurring between 3 weeks and 2 months after their infant's birth) at Hurley Children's Center.
This study was approved by Hurley Medical Center's Institutional Review Board (IRB #2170872).
Infant information obtained included sex assigned at birth and age, in days, at the onemonth well-child visit.
Maternal information obtained at the time of delivery included race or ethnicity, marital status, age, type of medical insurance, and residential address.
Maternal residential address was then geocoded to determine whether the mother lived within the city of Flint (i.e., Rx Kids eligible) or outside the city of Flint (i.e., Rx Kids ineligible).

Based on geocoded address (i.e., Flint or non-Flint) and timing of birth (i.e., before or after Rx Kids implementation in January 2024), mothers were classified into four groups for the difference-indifferences analysis: Pre-Rx Kids Flint, Pre-Rx Kids Non-Flint, Post-Rx Kids Flint, and Post-Rx Kids Non-Flint.

The EPDS assesses common depressive-and anxiety-related symptoms and difficulties during the past seven days. 23 Individual items are scored from 0 to 3, and responses are summed for a total score of 0-30, with higher scores reflecting greater symptom severity and PPD risk.

text.text: With strong psychometric properties, a cut-off score ≥ 13 has strong specificity (0.95) and adequate sensitivity (0.66) for identifying women who may meet criteria for postpartum depression. 24 A score ≥ 10 has lower specificity (0.84) but greater sensitivity (0.85).

text.text: For descriptive analyses, participants were categorized as follows: • Low risk for PPD: EPDS score ≤ 9

To assess the association between Rx Kids implementation and PPD risk, we used a difference-in-differences strategy to estimate the adjusted change in the probability of a clinically significant EPDS score among mothers residing in Flint after Rx Kids implementation relative to the change observed in the temporal and geographic comparison groups.

Linear probability models were fitted with a characteristic difference-in-differences interaction term between binary variables for maternal place of residence at the time of delivery (i.e., Flint versus non-Flint) and timing relative to program implementation (i.e., pre-Rx Kids versus post-Rx Kids).

In addition to the interaction term, models were adjusted for maternal age, marital status, race, Medicaid insured status, Flint residency status, visit month indicators to account for seasonality, and birthyear fixed effects to account for temporal trends.
This analysis was repeated with each of the other measures of PPD (i.e., the binary variable using EPDS scores below or > 10 and the EPDS total score).

text.text: The key assumption of the difference-in-differences specification was that outcomes would have evolved similarly for mothers within and just outside of Flint between 2022 and 2025 had it not been for the implementation of Rx Kids (the "parallel trends" assumption).

This assumption required that no other interventions occurred contemporaneously with Rx Kids in Flint; there were no other known population-level perinatal interventions targeting only mothers of infants born in the city of Flint between 2022 and 2025.
Additionally, our specification required no anticipatory effects and no endogenous selection effects.
To the extent that these assumptions hold, our results can be interpreted as causal impacts of Rx Kids.

To validate some of our assumptions, we also fit an event study specification for our primary outcome, which allowed us to test our parallel trends assumption in the pre-period and allowed for different treatment effects to be estimated for 2024 and 2025.
Additionally, we defined program exposure based on residency, not enrollment.
As such, we took an intent-to-treat approach in our analysis to capture the population-level effect of the program.

Over time, Rx Kids has shown high aggregate uptake rates in Flint, near 100% with greater than 90% of participants enrolling prenatally. 25 To preserve sample size, we included all observations after program launch (January 1, 2024), rather than applying weights or excluding the ramp-up period.

text.text: Due to high take-up rates, it is likely that our intent-to-treat estimates would be very close to estimates of overall treatment effects of the program itself.
All statistical tests were two-sided with a level of significance set at p < 0.05.
text.formatted: All statistical tests were two-sided with a level of significance set at p < 0.05.

text.text: Standard errors for all analyses were robust to heteroskedasticity.
We reported 95% CIs and standard pvalues for all outcomes.
All analyses were performed using Stata, version 19.0.
From January 1, 2022, to December 31, 2025, 815 infants born at Hurley Medical Center had a one-month well-child visit at the Hurley Children's Clinic.
Of these, 393 were born before January 1, 2024 (184 Flint, 209 non-Flint), and 422 were born on or after January 1, 2024 (211 Flint, 211 non-Flint), based on geocoded residential addresses.

Descriptively, changes in mean EPDS scores generally mirrored changes observed for the binary outcomes (Supplemental Figure 2).

text.text: In this quasi-experimental, difference-in-differences study, exposure to Rx Kids was associated with a 9.8-percentage-point reduction in the likelihood of screening at high risk for PPD on the EPDS among mothers of one-month-old infants.

Findings were consistent across multiple analyses, with Rx Kids-exposed mothers demonstrating lower rates of both high (EPDS ≥13) and moderate (EPDS ≥10) PPD risk, as well as lower mean EPDS scores, relative to comparison groups.

These results suggest that Rx Kids may improve maternal mental health across the distribution of depressive symptoms, rather than solely reducing the proportion of mothers exceeding clinically relevant screening thresholds.
Importantly, these findings also suggest a potential reduction in place-based maternal mental health disparities.
Before Rx Kids implementation, mothers in Flint, a community facing substantial socioeconomic challenges, had higher rates of elevated PPD risk than mothers in our comparison communities.
Following implementation, this pattern reversed, with Flint mothers demonstrating lower PPD risk than non-Flint mothers (Figure 1).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that place-based economic interventions may offer a promising strategy for improving maternal mental health and reducing disparities at the population level.
One plausible explanation for our findings is that Rx Kids reduced financial stress during a period of heightened economic vulnerability.

Pregnancy and infancy are accompanied by increased household expenses, disruptions to employment and income, and growing caregiving demands. 10, 26 By providing unconditional cash support, Rx Kids may reduce the stress associated with meeting basic needs, paying for household expenses, and purchasing infant supplies.

text.text: In support of this explanation, Rx Kids participant surveys (n=2,985) found that 85% of mothers said the program helped them become more financially secure and 88% of mothers reported reduced stress. 27 Additionally, qualitative studies have documented the close relationship between financial insecurity and maternal mental health along with a sense of relief and mental ease that comes with receiving cash support. 28, 29 The relationship between financial hardship and maternal mental health may also involve biological pathways.

[30] [31] [32] Thus, by reducing financial insecurity and associated stress, cash transfers may influence maternal mental health through both psychological and physiological mechanisms.

Research has linked inadequate prenatal care with increased risk of postpartum depressive symptoms. 33, 34 Prenatal care provides opportunities to promote healthy behaviors, connect mothers with supportive services, and offer social support during the critical perinatal period.

And my focus is strictly on them."

Another mother explicitly connected financial security and time at home with not experiencing postpartum depression: "I really didn't go through postpartum depression, because I wasn't worried about having no money...

I was just excited to stay home with my baby." 28 Together, these pathways suggest that unconditional perinatal cash support may influence maternal mental health through multiple, potentially reinforcing mechanisms.

text.text: Although the present study did not directly evaluate these mechanisms, the findings highlight the potential for perinatal economic interventions to address several underlying contributors to postpartum depression simultaneously.
Although numerous studies have examined the effects of cash transfers on mental health, far fewer have focused specifically on parental depression during the perinatal period.

To our knowledge, no prior study has evaluated a universal, unconditional perinatal cash transfer program in the United States in relation to postpartum depression (PPD) risk, and we are unaware of any published studies examining the impact of cash transfers on PPD risk using the EPDS.

Existing evidence has largely focused on other economic support policies, including expansions of the Child Tax Credit, unconditional cash transfers to mothers with low-income, and paid maternity leave.
The temporary expansion of the federal Child Tax Credit in 2021 provided near-universal eligibility and monthly postnatal cash payments to families with children.
Published studies examining its effects on parental depression have produced mixed findings.

Some found no significant effects, [35] [36] [37] while others reported reductions in depressive symptoms, particularly among low-income families and racial and ethnic minority populations. [38] [39] [40] [41] [42] Similarly, the Baby's First Years study provided postnatal child cash transfers to 400 mothers with low incomes who were randomized to receive $333 monthly; compared with mothers randomized to receive $20 monthly, those receiving $333 did not experience significant improvements in maternal depression. 43, 44 In contrast, our findings suggest that policies that reduce financial strain during early parenthood may be associated with improved maternal mental health outcomes.

text.text: Finally, our findings affirm and build on previous Rx Kids research demonstrating reductions in maternal depressive symptoms using the CES-D-10. 13 The current study finds similar reductions in PPD risk using electronic health record-derived EPDS data, a validated instrument specifically designed to screen for PPD during routine healthcare visits. 2, 23 The consistency in findings across screening instruments and data collection settings strengthens evidence that Rx Kids may improve maternal mental health and suggests that these effects may be detectable not only in research surveys but also in routinely collected clinical data.

text.text: Efforts to address PPD have traditionally focused on detection and treatment within healthcare settings.

While these approaches remain essential, our findings suggest that economic policies addressing perinatal financial insecurity may offer an important complementary strategy for improving maternal mental health.

Rather than intervening only after depressive symptoms emerge, policies that reduce financial and material hardship during the perinatal period may help prevent or mitigate upstream risk factors for PPD.
These findings support a broader approach to maternal mental health that extends beyond clinical care to address the socioeconomic conditions shaping maternal well-being.

The reversal of preexisting disparities in PPD risk between Flint and comparison communities suggests that place-based economic interventions may help reduce geographic and socioeconomic inequities in maternal mental health.
By providing universal support within participating communities, Rx Kids offers a population-level approach that does not depend on individual income eligibility or access to mental health services.
This model may be particularly relevant for communities experiencing concentrated poverty, where financial insecurity and barriers to healthcare often intersect.
Finally, our findings underscore the importance of recognizing maternal mental health as a key outcome of family economic policy.
Incorporating maternal mental health outcomes into evaluations of economic policies could provide a more comprehensive understanding of their health and societal benefits.

As policymakers consider strategies to improve maternal and infant health, universal economic support during pregnancy and infancy may warrant inclusion as part of a broader, prevention-oriented maternal health policy agenda.

Future research should examine whether these findings extend to other Rx Kids communities and identify the mechanisms through which cash support improves maternal mental health, including reduced financial stress, improved prenatal care, and increased maternal time affluence.
Longer-term studies should assess sustained maternal and child health outcomes and quantify potential downstream healthcare cost savings and broader economic returns.
Finally, evaluating the effects of program timing, payment amounts, duration, and universal eligibility could inform the design and expansion of perinatal economic support policies.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.

First, although the difference-in-differences design, adjustment for relevant covariates, and use of multiple comparison groups strengthen causal inference, residual confounding and unmeasured differences between exposed and unexposed mothers remain possible.
In addition, the validity of the difference-in-differences approach depends on the assumption that, in the absence of Rx Kids, PPD risk would have followed parallel trends in Flint and non-Flint.
Although event-study analyses supported this assumption, it cannot be definitively established.
Second, exposure to Rx Kids was inferred from maternal residence at birth and program timing rather than verified individual enrollment or receipt of payments.
Although prior evaluations indicate near-universal program uptake among eligible families, 25 some exposure misclassification is possible.

text.text: Third, the EPDS is a validated screening instrument that identifies elevated PPD risk but does not establish a clinical diagnosis. 23 Finally, analyses were limited to mothers who attended their infant's onemonth well-child visit and completed EPDS screening, potentially introducing selection bias and limiting generalizability to all postpartum mothers.

text.text: Findings from Flint may also not fully generalize to other communities with different demographic, socioeconomic, healthcare, or policy characteristics.
This study has several important strengths.

First, the quasi-experimental difference-indifferences design, supported by event-study analyses and multiple comparison groups, provides a rigorous approach to evaluating the effects of Rx Kids under real-world conditions.

Unlike interventions implemented within controlled research settings, Rx Kids is a universal, community-wide program, allowing us to rigorously examine the potential population-level effects of economic support during pregnancy and infancy.
Second, this study leveraged routinely collected clinical data from electronic health records rather than relying on incentivized surveys or self-reported program outcomes.

PPD symptoms were assessed using the validated EPDS during routine one-month pediatric wellchild visits, consistent with American Academy of Pediatrics screening recommendations. 2 This approach strengthens the clinical and policy relevance of the findings and demonstrates the value of using existing healthcare data for evaluating the health effects of economic interventions.

text.text: Third, the consistency of findings across multiple EPDS outcomes, including moderate and high PPD risk and mean depressive symptom scores, as well as with earlier Rx Kids research using a different depression screening instrument, 13 strengthens confidence in the observed association between program exposure and improved maternal mental health.

text.text: Finally, although conducted in a single Midwestern city, the study included a racially and socioeconomically diverse population experiencing intersecting social and structural disadvantages.

These characteristics make the findings particularly relevant to broader discussions of maternal health equity, the social and economic drivers of health, and the potential role of place-based economic policies in improving population health.

In this quasi-experimental, difference-in-differences study, exposure to Rx Kids was associated with a 9.8-percentage-point reduction in the likelihood of screening at high risk for PPD during routine one-month pediatric visits.

These findings reinforce the idea that PPD is not only a clinical concern but also a population health outcome shaped by the economic and social conditions in which women become pregnant, give birth, and care for their infants.

As the first evaluation of a universal, unconditional perinatal cash transfer program in the U.S. to examine PPD risk, this study suggests that economic support during the perinatal period may help improve maternal mental health and reduce place-based disparities.
